turn_text: And recently was announced that Montana will be moving into kind of an endemic approach to deal with COVID. What does that mean and what impact will that have for for Montanans?

Well, we're going to live with this for a while. And first, I just want to say thank you to all the medical workers who have been on the front lines for the last two years as we've suffered through this. But we've won. We're making progress and working with our medical staff at DPHHS. We all concluded that with the precipitous drop in hospitalizations, the number of infections going way down, and no variance of concern on the horizon, it was time to move away from a pandemic approach to an endemic approach. And what that means is we have other things that are endemic, like the flu is endemic, measles is endemic, smallpox is endemic. And so now, rather than mass, max, vacs, clinics, You're going to get the COVID vaccine from your doctor or the local pharmacy. The state's going to get out of the business of being in the middle of distributing PPE that's going to come through standard medical supply channels because the emergency is over and we can go back to normal. Now, we're going to stay nimble. We're going to monitor it probably not every day, but certainly weekly. And if there is a crunch somewhere, we'll tighten things back up again, but we're not going to go back to the unreasonable mandates that just didn't work. We're going to have to learn to live with this. People with underlying conditions should continue to take necessary precautions to protect their health. But my tenants are certainly smart enough to do that. This means the pandemic is over.
